title: Washington's Spectacles at Newburgh
text:
In March 1783 the Continental Army was camped at Newburgh, New York, waiting for a peace treaty with Britain. The officers had gone unpaid for months, and Congress seemed unable to keep its promises of pensions. An anonymous letter circulated in camp urging the officers to defy Congress, and possibly to march on it, if their demands were not met. Washington forbade the meeting the letter proposed and called one of his own for March 15, where he was not expected to appear.

On March 15 George Washington unexpectedly walked into the meeting hall. He gave a prepared speech asking the officers not to stain the honor they had won and to trust Congress to do them justice. The room remained cold.

He then began to read a letter from a congressman. He stumbled over the words, took out a pair of spectacles that few of his officers had ever seen him wear, and said, according to accounts of those present, that he had grown gray in the service of his country and was now growing blind. Several officers were moved to tears.

After he left, the officers voted to reject the anonymous call and to express their confidence in Congress. The threat of a military coup dissolved.
lesson: Showing honestly what your service has cost you can move people more than argument. Credibility built over years is what makes such a moment work.
source: Washington's address to the officers, March 15, 1783; accounts of officers present, including Samuel Shaw
caveat: The exact words about growing gray and blind differ slightly among the accounts of those present.
